column6: The commentary develops the owner, leading animal, pasture, and vulnerable wanderer within its herd imagery; the psalm names YHWH as shepherd and the speaker as a sheep who lacks nothing.
The commentary joins the service-path image to a later request for guidance; the shepherd psalm leads the sheep on right paths for his name’s sake.
The commentary pictures a worn traveler needing support and asks God for help; the psalmist walks through a deadly valley with the shepherd’s rod and staff as comfort.
The commentary contrasts a community that knows its owner with strays who lose the way; Ezekiel pictures YHWH searching for scattered sheep and rescuing them from where they have wandered.
The commentary’s root imagery includes the lost traveler and the herd animal gone astray; YHWH promises to seek the lost, bring back the strayed, bind the injured, and strengthen the weak.
The commentary’s augment links direct address to God’s answer to those who call; the psalm says YHWH hears those who call on him and saves them.

column5: our eyes on you for help
column6: The commentary makes the aid request a separate act addressed to God; Jehoshaphat prays for the whole people, “we do not know what to do, but our eyes are on you.”
The commentary leaves the need for help open while making God its sole source; after the communal plea, Judah is told to stand and see the salvation YHWH will give.
The commentary describes the human speaker as belonging to the Lord of all creation; the psalm says the earth and all who dwell in it belong to YHWH.
The commentary says worship is addressed to God alone; Isaiah’s oracle has every knee bow to YHWH and every tongue swear allegiance to him.
The commentary recalls Moses asking God for Aaron’s help in the mission to Pharaoh; in Exodus God appoints Aaron to meet Moses and assist him as spokesman.

column5: God helps through a human agent
column6: The commentary distinguishes asking God for help from receiving human assistance; God tells Moses to speak with Aaron and promises to help both of them speak.

column5: life and death belong to the Lord
column6: The commentary says a person belongs to God beyond scheduled acts of worship; Paul says that whether believers live or die, they belong to the Lord.
The commentary puts worship and asking aid side by side; Paul tells the community to bring every request to God with thanksgiving, joining petition to praise.
The commentary says worship is a continuing state and can be spoken in prayer; Hebrews calls believers to offer a continual sacrifice of praise through their lips.
The commentary moves from “we ask you for aid” to the next verse’s request for guidance; James tells anyone lacking wisdom to ask God, who gives generously.
The commentary leaves the aid requested open to every need; Peter tells believers to cast their anxieties on God because he cares for them.
The commentary reads “we” as a community that reaches beyond a solitary worshipper; Revelation gathers a multitude from every nation before the throne and the Lamb.
The commentary notes that the soul is first welcomed among God’s servants before entering the garden; Revelation depicts the gathered multitude serving God before his throne day and night.
The commentary develops the lost traveler, the herd, and the need for guidance and help; Revelation depicts the Lamb as shepherd leading the people to springs of living water.
The commentary places the community among God’s servants before naming the garden; Revelation’s final city is where God’s servants worship him and see his face.
The commentary says people or other means may assist while God remains the one ultimately asked for help; Hebrews describes angels as spirits sent to serve those who inherit salvation.
The commentary joins aid to worship and prayer; Paul says the Spirit helps believers in weakness and intercedes when they do not know how to pray.
The commentary evokes the strayed herd animal and the traveler who cannot find the way; Jesus’ parable has a shepherd leave the ninety-nine to search for one lost sheep.
The commentary’s image of a vulnerable traveler needing support is made concrete when the shepherd finds the lost sheep, puts it on his shoulders, and carries it home.
The commentary describes asking God for aid across all needs; Revelation says the gathered servants will hunger and thirst no more under the Lamb’s care.
The commentary distinguishes God as the one asked for help from those who can serve as instruments; Hebrews presents angels as agents sent to aid the heirs of salvation.
